What a root is. Almost every Arabic word is built from a root of three or four consonants. The root ك ت ب (k-t-b, writing) yields كِتاب (book), كَتَبَ (he wrote) and كاتِب (scribe) — so counting roots rather than words shows which ideas recur, not just which spellings.

How the counts were made. Each of the 77,429 words of the Qur'an is tagged with its root in the Quranic Arabic Corpus morphological annotation, and the figures here are a straight tally of those tags. The remaining 27,160 words are particles and pronouns (مِن, فِى, ٱلَّذِين) that carry no root, so they do not appear below however frequent they are.

Glosses are short indications of a root's core sense rather than translations, and cover 229 roots: the 100 most frequent, plus the leading roots of each letter group below. Surah names are the ones used in Al-Quran.html, with the common English name alongside.

Letter-group diagrams

The first four size letters by how often their roots occur. Prophets and Names keep the theme wheel and draw a line from each letter group to a name — solid if the name begins with that letter, dashed if the corpus tags the name with a root from that group. Names includes every proper name the corpus marks, plus Dhul-Qarnayn (split across two words, so not a single name tag). Switch diagrams with the buttons.

Roots grouped by first letter

Each letter gathers every root that begins with it. The theme is a three-word summary of those roots' senses — letters themselves have no meaning. Click a row to open the sense clusters inside that group; roots still without a gloss sit unlabelled at the end.
